=== 6. COMPETING EXPLANATIONS NOT CONTROLLABLE OVER THE PERIOD THAT DRIVES THE RESULT ===
Algorithmic trading. Weller, "Does Algorithmic Trading Reduce Information Acquisition?", Review of Financial Studies 31(6), 2018, 2184–2226, uses the SAME price-jump ratio and finds information in prices falls 9–13% per standard deviation of AT activity, up to a month before scheduled disclosures. AT penetration rose over roughly 1995–2012 — the window that drives Sammon's OLS. His MIDAS AT proxies exist only from 2012, so he CANNOT control for AT over the period generating his result, and on the 2012–2019 window where he can, his |Ret| coefficient is insignificant. Worse, the AT controls behave incoherently in Table C1: Cancel-to-Trade (positively correlated with AT) enters NEGATIVELY on |Ret|, |Ret|/SD, PJ and IVD — i.e. more AT implies MORE pre-announcement informativeness, the opposite of Weller's finding on Weller's own measure. Odd Lot Ratio flips sign across measures. The proxies are evidently picking up liquidity/size, so the "AT is not driving my results" claim is unsupported.
Reg FD (Aug 2000). Sammon's test drops pre-2001 data and calls the result "quantitatively similar." The |Ret| coefficient falls from 0.0635 to 0.0463, a 27% drop from removing one third of the sample — a meaningful attenuation, not similarity. And the test does not address the actual threat, which is a Reg-FD-induced level shift that differs across firms in ways correlated with passive ownership; year-quarter FE absorb the common component only.
Decimalization (2001). ZERO mentions of "decimaliz" or "tick size" in the manuscript. Tick-size reduction is a first-order, well-documented structural break in the profitability of informed pre-announcement trading, hitting in the same year as Reg FD and the same year as the |Ret|/SD acceleration. Not addressed at all.
Insider-trading enforcement. Sammon names it (citing Coffee 2007) as coinciding with the 2001 acceleration, then never tests it.
Four separate structural breaks — Reg FD, decimalization, insider-enforcement, AT — all cluster at the same inflection point he attributes to passive ownership, and none is controllable over the period that generates the estimate.

=== 7. MEASUREMENT AND SAMPLE-SELECTION ===
PJ: the Weller non-event filter deletes 54.5% of announcements, and the deletion is size-correlated (Sammon refuses to value-weight PJ for this reason). N drops from 441,238 to 150,113.
IVD: OptionMetrics begins 1996, and coverage is limited to option-listed equities — under half the sample (112,084 obs). That subsample is skewed toward large, liquid, high-passive firms, so the one genuinely independent measure is estimated on the most selected sample.
Passive ownership: built from CRSP MF + ETF matched via MFLINKS to Thomson S12. Securities never appearing in S12 are IMPUTED AS ZERO passive ownership — a systematic, time-varying error given documented S12 coverage deterioration. Monthly values are LINEARLY INTERPOLATED between quarter-ends, so the pre-announcement passive share partly reflects holdings measured AFTER the announcement (mitigated: he reports results unchanged using last-reported level). The measure also captures only explicitly labeled passive funds, missing internal indexing and closet indexing — Sammon invokes this in footnote 16 to excuse the IV being 3–4x the OLS, i.e. he uses a known measurement failure as an explanation for an anomalous result rather than as a limitation.

=== 8. VERSION DRIFT (four drafts, five years) ===
Apr 2020, "Earnings Announcements and the Rise of Passive Ownership," 1990–2018: three measures — pre-earnings abnormal volume, pre-earnings drift, share of annual volatility on earnings days. No percentage headline. Mechanism: fewer analysts, fewer SEC downloads.
Nov 2021, retitled "Passive Ownership and Price Informativeness," 1990–2018: "three new empirical measures." No percentage headline. Mechanism: "investors expend less effort gathering information."
Mar 2023, 1990–2018: headline "roughly 16%." Mechanism in abstract: less information collection plus limits to arbitrage. Contains a full Section 5 "Mechanisms" with five subsections (5.1 systematic vs idiosyncratic news, 5.2 information gathering, 5.3 sell-side analyst coverage, 5.4 pre-earnings abnormal turnover, 5.5 equilibrium response of non-passive investors).
Oct 2023 = published Management Science version, 1990–2019: headline becomes "approximately 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation." The ENTIRE Section 5 Mechanisms is DELETED, and the mechanism claim is REMOVED from the abstract.
So across drafts the measure set was replaced, the headline grew from 16% to 25% on a one-year sample extension plus a change of normalization, and the evidence for the causal channel was cut. Fragments survive in appendices D.7/D8, but reframed as exclusion-restriction checks — and there, as noted in §3, the analyst/attention results point the WRONG WAY for the mechanism in the S&P experiment. The published paper therefore offers no affirmative mechanism evidence for why passive ownership would cause the effect.

=== WHAT SURVIVES ===
The DESCRIPTIVE fact is solid and independently corroborated: over 1990–2019, absolute announcement-day returns rose relative to pre-announcement returns and relative to pre-announcement volatility; |Ret|/SD went from about 1.0 to about 3.5, PJ from about 0.2 to over 0.5. Beaver–McNichols–Wang (JAE 2020) document the same phenomenon with different data and different measures. What does NOT survive is the attribution to passive ownership and the "one quarter of the mean" magnitude.

=== WHY VETO RATHER THAN RESTRICTED_USE ===
Any single one of these would be a RESTRICTED_USE. The combination is disqualifying for load-bearing use, because the failures are not independent — they all point the same way. The confound that the measures cannot exclude (more news at the announcement) is affirmatively PRESENT in the author's own Table D5. The literature that documents that confound as the leading explanation of the same time series is not cited once. And the effect is absent in exactly the recent, high-passive-ownership data where the causal mechanism predicts it should be strongest. A number that is (i) a hand-averaged composite of four collinear ratios, (ii) OLS with the aggregate trend fixed-effected out and then applied to an aggregate trend, (iii) insignificant on the last third of its own sample, (iv) cut roughly in half by three more years of data, and (v) backed by an "almost always insignificant" reduced form with no parallel-trends evidence anywhere, cannot be the strongest pillar of an argument that a price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated because of passive investing. If it is the strongest evidence available, the honest conclusion the article should draw is that the evidence is weak — not that the deterioration is established at one quarter of the mean.

reasoning:
BOTTOM LINE: Sammon's finding is NOT single-source, but it is also not multi-source-confirmed in the way the article wants. The literature splits cleanly along a seam: independent teams CONFIRM the mechanism claim (passive ownership lowers the firm-specific/private-information content of prices) and CONFIRM the descriptive timing fact (pre-announcement anticipation weakened over 1990-2019), but independent teams using Sammon's OWN two instruments reach null or opposite-signed conclusions about whether this constitutes deterioration of price discovery. Several read the identical reallocation of return variance into the announcement window as markets getting BETTER, not worse. That is a genuine direction contest on the claim the article is leaning on.

=== A. GENUINELY INDEPENDENT SAME-DIRECTION MEASUREMENTS (mechanism claim) ===

A1. Höfler, Schlag & Schmeling, "Passive Investing and Market Quality" (working paper, March 2025 version; AFA 2025, SFS Cavalcade 2024; Goethe Univ. Frankfurt / SAFE / CEPR). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/hss.txt. Fully independent team, different measure family (Brogaard, Nguyen, Putniņš & Wu (2022) return-variance decomposition), overlapping-but-differently-implemented identification (Russell 2000 assignment IV with Appel-Gormley-Keim banding controls), data 2000-2020 (extends one year past Sammon). Per SD of passive ETF ownership (Table IA, bandwidth 300, N=17,193): FirmInfo variance share −8.01 (t=−2.82); PrivateInfo share −10.2 (t=−3.42); Noise share +6.09 (t=3.88); MktInfo +1.93 (t=0.76, insig.); PublicInfo +2.18 (t=0.90, insig.). Alternative horizon spec: PrivateInfo −13.73 (t=−4.10). This is the single strongest independent confirmation available, because "PrivateInfo share falls, MktInfo unchanged" is precisely Sammon's proposed channel (passive owners collect less firm-specific information) measured without any earnings-announcement window at all.

A2. Bennett, Stulz & Wang, "Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?" (NBER w27593, 2020; published JFE). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/bsw.txt. Independent team, 1997-2017, S&P 500 additions with matched controls, firm+year FE, firm-clustered SEs. Two measures, neither earnings-based: Rsq (market-model R²) and GPIN (Duarte-Hu-Young generalized PIN). Panel A: SP500Add → Rsq +0.022 (t=2.81); GPIN −0.021 (t=−3.95). Panel B regresses informativeness directly on passive holdings: no link for Rsq, strong negative link for GPIN. Sammon himself benchmarks against this (his §"comparison with the literature"): a 24% passive-ownership increase → GPIN decline of ~0.09 vs GPIN mean 0.07 / SD 0.17 — i.e., BSW's implied effect is LARGER than Sammon's, "same order of magnitude."
IMPORTANT CAVEAT I found in BSW that Sammon does not surface: BSW's GPIN effect "decreases significantly less in the late period" (Late = 2008+), which they call "a weaker treatment effect of index addition on price informativeness." The attenuation is in exactly the sub-period when passive ownership grew fastest — a time-series pattern in tension with Sammon's "rise in passive over 30 years caused the decline" extrapolation. BSW also find no effect of index addition on investment efficiency in the late period.

A3. Israeli, Lee & Sridharan, "Is there a dark side to exchange traded funds? An information perspective," Review of Accounting Studies 22(3), 2017, 1048-1083. Independent team, ETF-ownership panel, four outcomes: higher bid-ask spreads, higher return synchronicity, LOWER future earnings response coefficients (FERC), fewer analysts. The FERC result is the closest independent analogue to Sammon's construct — FERC literally measures the degree to which today's price already impounds future earnings, i.e. pre-announcement anticipation — and it moves the same way. Sammon distinguishes himself from ILS (his fn.2) by saying ILS study the "contemporaneous relationship... conditional on a given amount of information being released," but the FERC test is not contemporaneous and does corroborate him.

A4. Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg, "On index investing," JFE 145(3), 2022 — PARTIAL/upstream confirmation only. Independent team, Russell RDD. They confirm the INPUT channel: Google search volume −3.8%, EDGAR page views −14.1%, analyst reports −10.8% with more index investing. But see C1 — their price-side result is a null.

=== B. INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF THE DESCRIPTIVE TREND, WITH A NON-PASSIVE ATTRIBUTION ===

B1. Martineau, "Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift," Critical Finance Review (accepted; Univ. of Toronto), sample 1984-2019. Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/martineau.txt. This is the most consequential thing I found. Martineau independently documents that "pre-announcement drifts have also significantly weakened over time" — Sammon's core descriptive fact, from a different team with a different research question — AND that announcement-day price response is 6x (all-but-microcap) and 3x (microcap) more responsive to earnings surprises in 2016-2019 than in 1984-1990, with PEAD gone since 2006 for all-but-microcap and announcement-date prices now a martingale w.r.t. one-quarter-ahead prices. He explicitly tests and rejects the pre-announcement channel as the explanation: "A weakening in pre-announcement drifts does not explain the improvement in the response of announcement date returns to earnings surprises." His conclusion is the opposite welfare sign from Sammon's: "stock prices have become more efficient following earnings announcements." Same reallocation of price discovery into the announcement window; passive investing is not part of his explanation at all.

B2. Beaver, McNichols & Wang, "Increased market response to earnings announcements in the 21st century: An empirical investigation," Journal of Accounting and Economics 69(1), 2020, sample 2001-2016. Independent team documenting the rise in announcement-day return variability and volume — the same trend that drives Sammon's |Ret| series — and attributing a substantial fraction of it to CONCURRENT information bundled INTO the announcement: management guidance, disaggregated financial-statement line items, and analyst forecasts released at the announcement. Their diagnostic is decisive: market response to guidance issued SEPARATELY from earnings DECLINED over the same period, while bundled guidance rose. That is a passive-free, mechanically-evidenced alternative generator of Sammon's headline trend. Sammon does not cite this paper anywhere in the October 2023 draft (I grepped; no Beaver citation).

B3. Weller, "Does Algorithmic Trading Reduce Information Acquisition?" RFS 31(6), 2018, 2184-2226; 54,879 stock-quarters of SEC MIDAS data. Same PJ price-jump measure Sammon adopts. Information in prices falls 9-13% per SD of algorithmic-trading activity, "up to a month before scheduled disclosures." Independent team, different data, same measure, same direction on the outcome — but a competing attribution. Sammon addresses this (App. C.2.2) by adding Weller's four AT proxies as controls, coefficients survive; but MIDAS starts in 2012, so the AT control is available for only 8 of his 30 years and cannot speak to the 1990-2012 trend that carries most of his time-series identification.

=== C. GENUINELY INDEPENDENT OPPOSITE-DIRECTION / NULL MEASUREMENTS ===

C1. Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (JFE 2022), price side. Russell reconstitution RDD — the SAME instrument family as Sammon's first IV, and Sammon explicitly follows their sample-construction procedure (he cites Coles et al. 2022 six times for method). They find NO effect across "a range of measures of price informativeness, including anomaly mispricing and post-earnings announcement drift," and characterize their tests as well-powered. Their conclusion: "the fraction and effort of informed investors adjust so that the relation between price and fundamental value is unchanged." That is a direct null on the outcome using the same identification, from the team whose methodology Sammon borrows. Sammon lists them as the one paper finding "no relationship" and moves on.

C2. Hu & Liang, "Passive Institutional Ownership and the Informational Efficiency of Stock Prices," Journal of Accounting, Auditing & Finance, published online 23 March 2026 (DOI 10.1177/0148558X261435231). Independent team, identification = S&P 500 additions — Sammon's SECOND IV. They ACCEPT that passive reduces pre-announcement informativeness and then show, on the same shock, that passive → greater firm disclosure, HIGHER earnings response coefficients, and WEAKER PEAD. Their synthesis is explicitly the opposite reading of Sammon's own configuration: less pre-announcement leakage + more complete incorporation at the announcement + less drift = better information environment. This is the sharpest available demonstration that Sammon's measured facts do not pin down his sign.

C3. Glosten, Nallareddy & Zou, "ETF Activity and Informational Efficiency of Underlying Securities," Management Science 67(1), 2021, 22-47. Independent team. ETF trading INCREASES informational efficiency, "resulting from the timely incorporation of systematic earnings information," concentrated in stocks with weak information environments and imperfectly competitive markets. Note the interpretive collision: Sammon cites GNZ as roughly corroborating him ("going from bottom to top decile of ETF ownership increases earnings response by 0.11 vs. average 0.240... similar magnitude to my estimate"), but GNZ read that same increased earnings response as efficiency IMPROVING. Identical coefficient, opposite welfare sign. HSS's decomposition arbitrates partly in GNZ's favor: MktInfo share is unchanged/positive while only PrivateInfo falls.

C4. Choi, "The Conditional Price Efficiency of Passive Investing" (SSRN 5480703, April 2026) and the related "Complementarity of Passive and Active Investment on Stock Price Efficiency." Independent author, Russell reconstitution IV — again Sammon's own instrument. Finds instrumented passive increases produce "economically large improvements in price efficiency" in firms with substantial active mutual-fund ownership, and negligible effects where active ownership is thin. Since passive ownership is highest in large caps, which are also the most actively covered, this cuts against extrapolating Sammon's average effect to the market-cap-weighted market.

C5. Kacperczyk, Sundaresan & Wang, "Do Foreign Institutional Investors Improve Price Efficiency?" RFS 34(3), 2021, 1317-1367 (NBER w24765, 2018 — this is the "Kacperczyk et al. (2018b)" Sammon rebuts in his fn.8). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/ksw.txt. International panel 2000-2013, MSCI additions + JGTRRA as ownership shocks. VERSION-DRIFT FINDING: Sammon's rebuttal quotes PJ coefficients (MSCI −0.041, JGTRRA −0.225 on Weller's price-jump measure) from that paper, but I could not locate the Weller PJ measure in either the 2018 NBER working paper or the published RFS article — neither contains the string "Weller" or "price jump." The published paper's primary measure is the Bai-Philippon-Savov predicted-cash-flow-variation PI, with PEAD as a robustness check. So the opposite-signed PJ estimate Sammon argues against appears to have been dropped between drafts, and the surviving published result on passive is a NULL: "the effects for passive ownership are largely insignificant" (their §5.1, three-year horizon; passive there = index funds/ETFs plus pension funds, banks, insurers, a broader construct than Sammon's). Anyone repeating Sammon's fn.8 should not cite it as a live opposite-sign result, and anyone citing KSW against Sammon should say "null," not "opposite."

C6. Kacperczyk, Nosal & Sundaresan, "Market Power and Price Informativeness," Review of Economic Studies 92(3), May 2025 (local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/kns.txt, July 2024 version). This is now a pure THEORY paper — no PJ empirics survive. Its model prediction is mixed for Sammon: informativeness is decreasing in the size of the passive sector (supports him) but non-monotonic in oligopolist size and decreasing in concentration (a competing driver over the same 30 years, since ownership concentration rose sharply alongside passive). Their dominant channel is information pass-through, not learning.

C7. Bai, Philippon & Savov, "Have financial markets become more informative?" JFE 122(3), 2016, 625-654. Independent team, 1960-2014, welfare-based measure (predicted variation of future cash flows from prices). Informativeness ROSE at 3-5 year horizons, and the rise is "concentrated among firms with greater institutional ownership and share turnover, firms with options trading, and growth firms" — i.e., concentrated where passive ownership is highest. Sammon acknowledges this (his fn.6) and argues compatibility via a Campbell-Shiller decomposition. The reconciliation is coherent but it is his own, not independently tested, and it means the two literatures never meet on a common measure.

C8. Farboodi, Matray, Veldkamp & Venkateswaran, "Where Has All the Data Gone?" RFS 35(7), 2022, 3101-3138 (lead article). Independent team. Large growth-firm prices increasingly reflect future earnings; small and value firms flat or declining. The cross-sectional gradient runs the WRONG way for Sammon's mechanism: passive ownership is most concentrated in exactly the large-cap firms whose prices became MORE informative about future fundamentals. Sammon does not cite this paper (grepped; no Farboodi citation in the Oct-2023 draft). It is arguably the sharpest cross-sectional contradiction available and it went unaddressed.

C9. López Vilaró, "Index Fund Ownership and Stock Price Efficiency: Evidence from Quarterly Earnings Seasons" (Univ. of Arkansas dissertation, 2023). On-point but low-weight: finds competing effects (lower investor disagreement around announcements = better; reduced peer-information incorporation = worse) and concludes "no conclusive evidence on the total impact of index fund ownership at currently observed levels."

=== D. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE ARTICLE ===
The article's framing — "the strongest evidence that SOME price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated" — survives only in its narrowest form. Defensible: the private/firm-specific-information share of price formation declines with passive ownership, confirmed by three independent teams on three different measures (HSS variance decomposition, BSW GPIN, ILS FERC). Not defensible: presenting Sammon's pre-announcement result as a clean, corroborated deterioration finding. Two independent teams running Sammon's own instruments (CHR on Russell, Hu-Liang on S&P 500 additions, plus Choi on Russell) get null or improvement; two independent teams (Martineau, Beaver et al.) reproduce his descriptive trend and attribute it to faster announcement-day processing and to more information being bundled into announcements; and the paper GNZ that Sammon counts in his favor reads its own coefficient as an efficiency gain.

BOTTOM LINE: The DIRECTION of the claim ("total passive ownership substantially exceeds the fund-based/ICI number") is independently corroborated by at least four genuinely independent teams using four different datasets, including one transaction-level study that directly observes who trades index rebalancings. The specific US LEVEL of 33.5% remains single-sourced to Chinco & Sammon; independent measurements of the same quantity span roughly 17.5% to 41%, with 33.5% sitting inside that range but not pinned by anyone else. Recommend UPGRADE_MULTISOURCE on the direction/multiplier, with the level explicitly attributed.

=== INDEPENDENT SAME-DIRECTION MEASUREMENTS (different team AND different data) ===

(1) STRONGEST — Escobar, Pandolfi, Pedraza & Williams, "Who Trades Index Rebalancings? Evidence on Benchmarking and Inelastic Demand," GWU Center for Economic Research WP 2026-008, May 11 2026 (Banco de la Republica de Colombia / Univ. of Naples Federico II+CEPR+CSEF / World Bank / GWU). Data: proprietary TRANSACTION-LEVEL records from the Bolsa de Valores de Colombia with investor-type identifiers, around MSCI international index additions/deletions (~2013-2017). Method: directly observes each trader rather than inferring from aggregate volume — a fundamentally different identification route from C&S's volume-inversion.
Findings verified in the primary text (local extract gwu.txt, lines 276-345):
 - "Among foreigners trading in the direction of the index on the implementation day, passive funds and ETFs purchase 0.87% of outstanding shares, while other foreign investors purchase 1.50%. Non-passive benchmarked investors, therefore, generate rebalancing-driven inflows that are 1.7 times larger than those of explicitly passive funds." → total/explicit multiplier = (0.87+1.50)/0.87 = 2.72x, i.e. MORE than C&S's ~2x.
 - "about 60% of trading by non-explicitly passive index trackers occurs on the implementation day" (vs 88% for declared passive funds) — independently confirms the behavioral premise that undeclared benchmarked money rebalances on reconstitution day alongside index funds.
 - Abstract: "Index demand extends beyond explicit index funds and ETFs: benchmarked but nominally active foreign institutions account for most rebalancing-driven trading."
 - They cite C&S once, in passing, as consistent (line 155) — this is corroboration, not a replication attempt.
CAVEATS: Colombian equities, emerging market, foreign institutional investors, MSCI (not the five US indexes), small event count. Validates the MECHANISM and the MULTIPLIER, not the US 33.5% level.
NOTE FOR METHOD_AUDIT SEAT: the same paper finds "Domestic investors absorb most of the shock, while arbitrage capital plays only a limited role" — i.e. the other side of reconstitution-day volume is decidedly NOT passive. That bears on whether counting total reconstitution-day volume double-counts.

(2) Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche, "How Competitive Is the Stock Market? Theory, Evidence from Portfolios, and Implications for the Rise of Passive Investing," American Economic Review 115(3), March 2025, pp. 975-1018 (UCLA / UCLA-Stockholm / Minnesota). Data: 13F institutional holdings. Method: Koijen-Yogo demand system; "passive" = investors with estimated fixed price elasticity below kappa=0.06 — a price-insensitivity construct, entirely orthogonal to reconstitution volume.
Finding: passive share of the US stock market rose from 19% (2000) to 41% (2020). C&S's own 2020 figure is 32.19% (JFE Table 3). Same direction, HIGHER magnitude, both roughly 2-3x the ICI fund-based number.
CAVEATS: the working-paper text states kappa=0.06 was chosen "to calibrate the level of passive investing," so the LEVEL is partly anchored to an external target while the GROWTH is measured. Also "price-insensitive" is a broader construct than "index-tracking" — it would sweep in buy-and-hold and inattentive holders who are not benchmarked to anything. Independent of C&S on team, data, and method; weaker as a level corroboration than as a direction corroboration.

(3) S&P Dow Jones Indices, Annual Survey of Assets (figures as of Dec 31, 2024, spglobal investor factbook). Data-generating process: S&P DJI client-reported licensee survey plus third-party data — completely independent of both volume and 13F holdings.
Findings: $12.999T INDEXED to the S&P 500 alone; $20.161T indexed-or-benchmarked to the S&P 500; $16.596T indexed across all S&P DJI indices. Survey scope explicitly covers "institutional funds, ETFs, retail mutual funds, exchange-traded derivatives, and other investable products" — i.e. it reaches institutional index mandates the ICI number omits.
Arithmetic cross-check: $13.0T against a ~$63T US total market cap at end-2024 is ~20.6% of US market cap indexed to ONE index family — already above the ICI all-index-fund share for the same year. That is an independent demonstration that indexed money exceeds the fund-based number.
Direct comparison to C&S: for Dec 31 2021 the same survey reported ~$7.1T indexed (of ~$15.6T indexed-or-benchmarked) to the S&P 500. Against ~$48.5-53T US market cap that is 13.4-14.6%, versus C&S's S&P-500 line of 16.80% for 2021 (JFE Table 3 decomposition: S&P500 16.80 + S&P MidCap400 1.12 + Russell1000 10.77 + Russell2000 1.06 + Nasdaq100 3.76 = 33.50). C&S run ~15-25% hot relative to the index provider's own indexed-assets survey — same ballpark, C&S on the high side. Since the survey undercounts (non-response; unlicensed internal indexing), this is consistent rather than contradictory, but it does not independently support the high end.
CAVEAT: "indexed" includes exchange-traded derivatives notional and non-US-domiciled vehicles, which inflate it as a measure of cash-equity ownership.

(4) BlackRock ViewPoint, Novick, Madhavan, Sethi, Matthews, Cohen & Bunzel, "Index Investing Supports Vibrant Capital Markets," Oct 2017. Data: WFE, SIFMA, ECB, BIS, HFR, Cerulli, Simfund, McKinsey (Dec 2016). Exhibit 2, verified from the primary PDF:
 Index = $11.9T = 17.5% of $67.9T global equity, decomposed: index mutual funds 3.4% + ETFs 4.0% + institutional indexing 7.9% + internal indexing 2.1%. Fund-only (MF+ETF) = 7.4%. Total/fund multiplier = 2.36x — MORE than double, from an independent industry accounting.
 US-specific (Exhibit 3, Dec 2016): index mutual funds 6.3% + ETFs 6.1% = 12.4% of US equity market.
INCENTIVE NOTE (cuts FOR the claim): BlackRock's rhetorical goal in that ViewPoint was to argue indexing is SMALL — its own headline is "index investing comprises less than 20% of global equities." An interested party biased toward a small number still produced a 2.36x multiplier over fund-only assets. That is incentive-compatible corroboration.

*** CITATION ERROR FOUND IN THE LOAD-BEARING PAPER ITSELF *** — C&S's JFE text states: "A 2017 BlackRock report put the passive-ownership share at 25.6% (Novick et al., 2017)." That is a misreading. In BlackRock Exhibit 2, 25.6% is the ACTIVE share ($17.4T); the index share is 17.5% ($11.9T); non-managed is 57.0%. Verified line-by-line against the primary PDF. This matters because C&S use that 25.6% to argue market participants already knew the number was well above 16% — the actual figure they are citing says 17.5% globally. It does not touch the 33.5% estimate itself (the misquote is in the framing of prior literature), but the article should NOT repeat "BlackRock said 25.6%" as corroboration; the correct BlackRock number is 17.5% global with a 2.36x multiplier.

(5) Cremers, Ferreira, Matos & Starks, "Indexing and Active Fund Management: International Evidence," Journal of Financial Economics 120(3), 2016. Data: worldwide mutual fund holdings. Method: Active Share (Cremers-Petajisto). Finding: "about 20% of the worldwide mutual fund assets are managed by closet indexers" (Active Share threshold), alongside explicitly indexed funds at ~22% of equity fund assets by 2010 — closet indexing is comparable in size to explicit indexing, an independent-method result supporting an approximate doubling within the fund universe.
CAVEATS: share of FUND-INDUSTRY assets, not market cap; worldwide not US; 2010 not 2021; excludes internal indexing by pensions/SWFs entirely.

=== MEASUREMENTS THAT LAND LOWER (magnitude tension, NOT direction contradiction) ===

(6) Pavlova & Sikorskaya, "Benchmarking Intensity," Review of Financial Studies 36(3), 2023, 859-903 (LBS). Holdings-based stock-level BMI; mean BMI ~0.159 in matched samples. Their own text concedes they lack data "for assets of benchmarked investors other than mutual funds and ETFs."

(7) Behmaram, "Indexing and the Elasticity of Stock Demand," April 2026 working paper. Indexing Inclusion Ratio (IXI): realized passive ownership from >17,000 funds' actual holdings across >570 benchmarks, adjusted for Active Share. Average IXI 13.4% in 2022-2023; unadjusted IXI_non-adj ~17%; BMI ~15.9%. He cites C&S approvingly ("actual passive ownership is approximately double self-declared index fund holdings") rather than contesting it, and his universe is fund holdings only.

(8) Bloomberg Intelligence (Seyffart 2023, as cited by C&S): "at least 19%" — above ICI's 16%, far below 33.5%.

WHY THESE DO NOT MAKE THIS DIRECTION_CONTESTED: (6), (7) and (8) all measure only the FUND universe — precisely the universe C&S argue is incomplete — so by construction they cannot rebut the claim that money outside that universe exists. But they carry a real cautionary signal for the article: every measurement that demands holdings-level documentation tops out around 13-17%; the gap between that and 33.5% is not observed in ANY holdings dataset. It is inferred from volume (C&S), from price elasticity (HHL), from survey self-report (S&P DJI, BlackRock), or from transaction records in a foreign market (Escobar et al.) — never from US holdings data. That is worth saying out loud in the article.

=== VERSION-DRIFT NOTE (relevant to how much weight the level can bear) ===
The 2022 working paper (local cs_2022.txt) headline: "passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020." The published JFE Table 3 gives 32.19% (SE 2.91) for 2020. The same year's estimate fell 5.6pp — roughly 2 standard errors — between working paper and publication. The article should quote only the published 33.5% (2021), never 37.8%.

=== CONCLUSION ===
UPGRADE_MULTISOURCE. Escobar-Pandolfi-Pedraza-Williams (2026) is the decisive addition: a different team, a different country, a different index family, and transaction-level investor identities rather than volume inference, independently finding that undeclared benchmarked money generates 1.7x the rebalancing demand of declared index funds (2.7x total multiplier). Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche (AER 2025) independently put US passive at 41% by 2020 via a demand system. BlackRock's own 2017 accounting implies a 2.36x multiplier. S&P DJI's survey shows one index family alone accounts for ~20% of US market cap in indexed assets. Nothing anywhere points the other way. The claim's DIRECTION is now well multi-sourced; the specific 33.5% figure is not, and should be attributed rather than stated as settled fact.

reasoning:
HOSTILE REFEREE REPORT — Sammon, "Passive Ownership and Price Informativeness," Management Science 71(6), June 2025, 4582–4598 (pre-pub: Oct 2023 WP, marcosammon.com; earlier drafts Nov 2021, Mar 2023).

Transcription is correct — the published MS abstract matches the audited wording ("approximately 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation"). The problem is not what the paper says; it is what the number is.

=== 1. IDENTIFICATION: THE "CAUSAL" IV IS PARTLY IDENTIFIED OFF A TIME TREND (most serious) ===
The IV is NOT the clean index-switch DiD it is presented as. Equations (5)–(6) use TWO excluded instruments: Post(i,t) and PassiveGap×Treated×Post. Post is a bare time indicator applying to treated AND control firms; the second-stage equation contains only Passive-hat and fixed effects, so Post is excluded. Sammon states this himself in Appendix D.5: "Recall that in Table 3, I am using both Post and Passive Gap×Treated×Post as instruments for passive ownership. Over my sample, there is a time trend toward increased passive ownership."

The exclusion restriction for Post is therefore: within a ±3-year window around each index-change cohort, the passage of calendar time affects |Ret|, |Ret|/SD, PJ and IVD ONLY through passive ownership. Over 1990–2019 that is untenable (Reg FD 2000, decimalization 2001, SOX, 8-K acceleration 2004, EDGAR/XBRL, guidance-practice change, the growth of algorithmic trading) and it is also circular: it assumes the paper's thesis in order to identify it.

The reduced form (Table D3) shows the arithmetic. The genuine quasi-experimental instrument, PassiveGap×Treated×Post, is insignificant in 7 of 8 specifications and WRONG-SIGNED in 2 of 8 (Russell PJ −0.31; S&P IVD −0.138). Russell |Ret|/SD is 1.61 with SE 6.955 — a ~[−12, +15] interval, zero information — yet the corresponding IV estimate is 11.68 (SE 2.352, t≈5). Post, by contrast, is positive and significant in 7 of 8. The 2SLS precision is coming from the trend instrument, not the experiment.

Sammon's defense misfires. He rebuts the Chernozhukov–Hansen (2008) "significant IV + insignificant RF = weak instruments" concern by pointing to first-stage F > 200 — but that F is dominated by Post (coefficient 0.02, SE 0.001, t≈20). A strong but invalid instrument is worse than a weak one; an F-statistic cannot answer an exclusion-restriction objection. The Lochner–Moretti (2004) t-ratio argument he invokes is derived for the JUST-IDENTIFIED single-instrument case and he concedes in the "Multiple Instruments" subsection that "the exact relationship between the IV and the reduced form is more complicated than the algebra above would imply." He then treats "Post is positive and significant" as confirmatory prediction (1) — but that is just the raw secular trend, consistent with any time-trending cause, and has no identifying content.

NO OVERIDENTIFICATION TEST IS REPORTED. With two instruments and one endogenous regressor the model is overidentified and a Hansen J / Sargan test is standard and free. I grepped the full paper: no "Hansen J", "Sargan", or "overidentif" anywhere. Given that the two instruments plainly disagree (trend instrument large-positive, experiment instrument ~zero/negative), a J-test would very likely reject. Its absence is the single most conspicuous omission in the paper.

Also conspicuous: Sammon runs a transparent two-way DiD (Post + Post×Treated, Eq. D9) for AUXILIARY outcomes (analyst coverage, attention, earnings volatility, Table D7) but NEVER for the four main outcomes. The simplest, most legible test of the index-switch experiment on the headline dependent variables is not shown anywhere.

Corollary: "IV is 2.5–4x OLS, therefore OLS is not biased by reverse causality" (Section 4.3) inverts the standard reading. A systematic 2.5–4x IV/OLS gap with a null reduced form on the experimental instrument is a textbook signature of exclusion-restriction violation, not of OLS attenuation.

=== 2. THE OLS HEADLINE IS A CROSS-SECTIONAL→TIME-SERIES EXTRAPOLATION ===
Table 2 includes YEAR-QUARTER fixed effects. Sammon: "The year-quarter fixed effects account for the time trends in pre-earnings announcement price informativeness." So β is identified purely WITHIN quarter, ACROSS firms — high-passive vs low-passive firm at the same date. The headline then multiplies that cross-sectional β by a 30-YEAR AGGREGATE change in passive ownership (15%, 1990→2019). The FE absorb the very trend the headline claims to explain, and the trend is reintroduced by multiplication. Nothing in a within-quarter firm comparison licenses an aggregate general-equilibrium counterfactual. Kacperczyk, Nosal & Sundaresan ("Market Power and Price Informativeness," 2022) show in an explicit GE model that price informativeness is NON-MONOTONIC in the size of the passive oligopolistic sector — so the linear extrapolation is not even theoretically supported.

=== 3. THE "~1/4" IS A COMPOSITE OF INCOMMENSURABLE RATIOS, WITH NO STANDARD ERROR ===
It is not an estimate. Sammon: "An equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' means is 0.23 (roughly 1/4th)." The four components are 0.20 (|Ret|, bps of return), 0.33 (|Ret|/SD, unitless), 0.10 (PJ, a fraction), 0.29 (IVD, vol points) — a 3.3x spread across units that cannot be averaged meaningfully. No SE, no CI, no delta-method. Critically, PJ — the measure Sammon himself says is "closer to measures of price informativeness that arise in Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) and Kyle (1985)" — gives the SMALLEST ratio, 0.10, less than half the headline. The headline is inflated by the two least theoretically-grounded measures.

WEIGHTING-BASIS MISMATCH: the 15% is the VALUE-weighted rise in passive ownership ("value weighted average passive ownership increased by 15% between 1990 and 2019"), but it is multiplied by EQUAL-weighted coefficients (Table 2 cols 1–4, Weight=Equal) and divided by EQUAL-weighted means (|Ret| mean 476bps; footnote 7 concedes the VW mean is 306bps). A consistently value-weighted composite is not even computable from the paper: PJ has no VW column at all ("I do not report a value-weighted version of Column 3"), and |Ret|/SD's VW coefficient falls 39% (4.425→2.717).

=== 4. ROBUSTNESS FAILURES THE ARTICLE MUST NOT IGNORE ===
(a) SAMPLE-END FRAGILITY. Sammon's own Appendix E extension to 1990–2022 cuts EVERY coefficient by 36–49%: |Ret| 0.0635→0.0386, |Ret|/SD 4.425→2.531, PJ 0.248→0.127, IVD 0.112→0.0714. The headline recomputed on 1990–2022 is roughly 1/8, not 1/4. His COVID-volatility rationalization explicitly covers only the three volatility-NORMALIZED measures ("for |Ret|/SD, PJ and IVD, there is a normalization") — it does not explain the 39% drop in |Ret|, which is not normalized. The 2019 cutoff is doing roughly half the work of the headline number, and the defense is a post-hoc story fitted after the extension broke the result.
(b) ALGORITHMIC-TRADING CONTROLS KILL THE HEADLINE MEASURE. Table C1: adding Weller's (2018) four MIDAS AT proxies drives the |Ret| coefficient to 0.0146 (SE 0.0143) and 0.0199 (SE 0.0139) — INSIGNIFICANT, and roughly a quarter to a third of the 0.0635 baseline. Sammon's text ("The point estimates are not significantly changed by including these controls") does not match his own table for |Ret|. |Ret|/SD survives but shrinks ~30% (4.425→3.264/2.951); PJ survives only weakly (0.236**/0.203*). Caveat in fairness: MIDAS exists only 2012–2019, so N falls 441,238→91,532 and power is reduced — but that is exactly why this cannot be cited as having ruled AT out.
(c) MULTIPLE TESTING. Four outcome measures × two index experiments × OLS/IV/RF/VW/subsample variants, with no multiplicity correction anywhere, and the headline is an average taken over the four measures after the fact.

=== 5. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY: THE MEASURES CANNOT SEPARATE THE TWO STORIES ===
All four measures are ratios of announcement-window price movement to pre-announcement price movement. They rise if less is anticipated beforehand (Sammon's reading) OR if MORE information is released at, and impounded on, the announcement date. Martineau ("Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift," Critical Finance Review) documents the second directly over the same period and the same event: PEAD has disappeared (non-existent for large stocks since 2006), announcement-date prices are now "martingale," and price responses to earnings surprises have INCREASED over time — "prices becoming more informative with respect to earnings surprises." Mechanically, a more complete, more compressed day-0 reaction raises |Ret|, |Ret|/SD and PJ exactly as Sammon's channel would. Martineau further finds pre-announcement drifts "significantly weakened over time" and names Reg FD as a leading cause. Same statistics, opposite interpretation, and the paper contains no test that discriminates between them.
Sammon's Reg FD defense is a stated prior, not evidence: "my prior is that information obtained in 2000 would not be relevant for more than a few years," plus reliance on year-quarter FE to absorb "level shifts." But Reg FD is not a level shift — it changed the mapping from analyst/institutional access to pre-announcement price movement, plausibly differentially for large, heavily-covered, index-member firms, i.e. precisely the high-passive-ownership firms. A post-2000 subsample with similar point estimates does not address a differential effect that persists throughout the post-2000 period.

=== 6. VERSION DRIFT (researcher degrees of freedom) ===
Three drafts, same author, same data, and the measure set was reconstructed twice while the headline grew:
• Nov 2021 (UConn WP): "three new empirical measures"; NO quantified headline in the abstract.
• Mar 2023 (HBS WP): four measures — QVS (quadratic variation share), DM, jump, IVD. Headline: "decline by roughly 16%," computed as 14.87/92.1, i.e. ONE measure (QVS) relative to its 1990 mean.
• Oct 2023 / MS 2025 published: QVS and DM DROPPED; |Ret| and |Ret|/SD ADDED; jump retained as PJ. Headline: "approximately 1/4th of its whole sample mean," now an equal-weighted average of FOUR ratios against WHOLE-SAMPLE means.
So both the construct set and the normalization convention changed on the path to publication, and the headline went none → 16% → 25%. The direction is stable across drafts; the magnitude is a moving target and should not be quoted as a precise measured quantity.

=== 7. AUTHOR INCENTIVES / COI ===
No financial COI found. Sammon is an academic (Associate Professor, HBS Finance; PhD Kellogg; previously Federal Reserve Bank of Boston), no disclosed industry or asset-manager relationship; the Mar 2023 draft acknowledges only Avi Nash Fund academic support. The relevant incentive is ordinary publication incentive toward a clean, quantified causal headline — which is visible in the drift documented in §6 and in the abstract's use of "has caused" to describe a magnitude computed from cross-sectional OLS with year-quarter FE.

=== 8. WHAT SURVIVES ===
Peer-reviewed at a top-5 journal. The DIRECTION is robust: the OLS association is positive and significant across all four measures, in both index experiments, in the post-2000 subsample, under value weighting (where reported), under the Crane–Crotty vs Appel-Gormley-Keim passive-ownership definitions, and stable in sign across three drafts and two different measure sets. The defensible finding is: firms with higher passive ownership have, cross-sectionally, a larger share of their earnings-related price movement occurring at the announcement rather than before it, and this association is present throughout 1990–2019.
What does NOT survive: the causal attribution (§1), the aggregate time-series counterfactual (§2), the specific "~1/4" magnitude (§3, §4a, §6), and the exclusion of algorithmic trading and Reg FD as alternative drivers of the time trend (§4b, §5).

=== VERDICT ===
RESTRICTED_USE, not VETO. Full veto would over-reach against a peer-reviewed result whose sign is genuinely robust. But the audited number as framed — "15% more passive ownership → pre-announcement informativeness falls by ~1/4 of its mean," causally attributed, used as the article's strongest evidence that a price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated — fails on identification, on units, and on sample robustness. It must not carry that weight. Conditions are enumerated in usageConditions; if the article cannot meet them, treat this item as vetoed and rebuild the section's evidentiary base.

The 29% is therefore not a decomposition of any observed phenomenon — it is a pure ceteris-paribus counterfactual asserting that passive flows added +29% relative while ~−46pp of unmodeled, unmeasured offsetting forces subtracted more. The same arithmetic on top-10 is worse: realized −2.0% cumulative versus an extrapolated passive contribution of +37.8%.

This is fatal for the article's intended use. An article citing this as evidence that "passive inflates the Mag 7" would be importing a number from a sample in which the megacaps LOST ground to the index, and whose only anchor for the counterfactual is a regression constant of −0.00137 that is statistically indistinguishable from zero (t = −0.54).

29.04% = 0.528% × (0.05/0.09) × 99. This cumulates a CONTEMPORANEOUS quarterly coefficient across 99 quarters, valid only if each quarter's price effect is permanent and additive. No long-horizon reversal test, no cumulative impulse-response, no test of permanence appears anywhere. If the effect fully mean-reverts the cumulative figure is ~0. The paper says "29%" and then, one sentence later, "the 30% estimate." Self-evidently an illustration, not a calibrated quantity.

The words "endogeneity," "reverse causality," and "exogenous" (in the empirical sense) never appear in connection with Table 6.2. The specification is contemporaneous OLS with no instrument. The reverse channel is strong and SAME-SIGNED: when megacaps lead, active managers — typically underweight megacaps — underperform the cap-weighted benchmark, which is a well-documented driver of flows into index funds. The controls (S&P500 return, lagged return, VIX) cannot absorb this, because the confounding variable IS the top-50-minus-index return, which is the dependent variable. Appendix E.3 regresses changes in index concentration on passive flows and presents this as corroboration. === FINDING 13: Construct validity of PassiveFlow — the naive critique is WRONG, the real one is not ===
In fairness to the authors: PassiveFlow_t = A_t/M_t − A_{t−1}/M_{t−1}. Since index funds hold the index, to first order Δ(A/M) ≈ (A/M)(f − n), where the index return CANCELS between numerator and denominator. So the "mechanically built from prices" objection is weaker than commonly asserted, and I decline to press it.

The residual term n (net issuance / index composition) is the real problem. Buybacks shrink M without shrinking A, mechanically RAISING measured PassiveFlow — and buybacks are megacap-dominated, procyclical, and have exceeded issuance since 2004 (falling S&P divisor). So the regressor is contaminated by a megacap-cash-flow term that independently correlates with megacap relative returns, in the same direction as the claimed effect. The paper never decomposes PassiveFlow into reported fund net flows versus issuance, and never uses CRSP/ICI reported net flows as a robustness check despite holding the data. This is a concrete, addressable, unaddressed flaw.

=== FINDING 14: Narrow measure breaks the extrapolation's internal scaling ===
The measure covers three ETFs (SPY, IVV, VOO) plus ICI S&P500 index mutual funds — 4.95pp of index cap over 25 years. It excludes total-market index funds, target-date funds, institutional internally-managed index mandates, and closet indexing; Chinco & Sammon (JFE 2024, "The passive ownership share is double what you think it is") put true passive share at roughly twice conventional estimates. The cumulation β×mean×99 is self-consistent ONLY if the narrow measure is a CONSTANT fraction of true passive flow. It demonstrably is not: non-S&P500 passive grew far faster than S&P500-specific passive over 1996–2020. The scaling assumption fails, biasing the 29% by an unknown amount in an unknown direction.

=== FINDING 15: Out-of-sample application to the Mag 7 ===
The sample ENDS 2020Q4. The Mag 7 concentration episode is 2023–2025; the term did not exist until 2023. Using a 1996–2020 estimate — from a window in which megacaps had NEGATIVE excess returns — to explain a post-2022 concentration surge is out-of-sample extrapolation onto precisely the period where the in-sample sign flipped. Nothing in this paper measures the Mag 7 era.

The paper acknowledges financial support from the LSE Paul Woolley Centre; Vayanos is a Centre co-director, and the Centre's research agenda is capital-market dysfunctionality, with Paul Woolley a longstanding public critic of benchmarked/index investing. This is a disclosed academic research prior, NOT a hidden or industry financial conflict, and RFS peer review is genuine mitigation. I weight it lightly. Newey-West with 3 lags on T=99 quarterly observations is thin but not unreasonable; the regressor is a differenced share, so the persistent-regressor/Stambaugh concern is muted. I do not press this.

The DIRECTION — passive flows are associated with megacap relative outperformance — has real support and I do not veto it: the main regression, the idiosyncratic-volatility panel (Table 6.3, lagged, double-clustered, t=2.45–2.53), the marginal S&P600 contrast, and most importantly the beginning-of-month quasi-natural-experiment (Table E.9), where 401(k) paycheck timing is plausibly exogenous to megacap returns and reproduces the SAME gradient shape (top-10 0.0282 t=2.28; top-50 0.0220 t=2.82; top-100 0.0140 t=2.10; top-150 and top-200 insignificant), with Firm×Month and Month×MonthStart fixed effects absorbing aggregate moves. Author incentives are low-to-moderate risk but non-zero and undisclosed to readers: Haddad "acknowledges financial support from the Fink Center for Finance and Investments at UCLA Anderson," a center endowed in 2008 by Laurence and Lori Fink ($10m); Larry Fink is founder/CEO of BlackRock, the world's largest passive manager. This does not impugn the work — the paper's other headline ("the stock market is far from the competitive ideal," 11% is "sizable") cuts against a whitewash reading, and both passive-critics and passive-defenders cite it. But the sentence most quoted in defense of passive ("competition offsets two-thirds") comes from a paper funded by a center endowed by the largest passive manager's founder. If the article makes this its keystone number it should carry the funding line. (The AER Author Disclosure Statement is listed as supplementary material; its contents were not retrievable from the article page.)

FATAL-ADJACENT PROBLEMS (these are why the number cannot stand unqualified):

A. THE HEADLINE IS 100% INSTRUMENT-DRIVEN, AND THE INSTRUMENT IS MODEL-GENERATED, NOT DESIGN-BASED. This is the single biggest finding of this audit and the article almost certainly does not know it. Table 2 row (15), "No instrument for Eagg": chi = 0.04 (s.e. 0.22). Row (16), "No instruments": chi = 0.63 (s.e. 0.29). Drop the aggregate-elasticity instrument and the strategic response is a statistical zero. At chi = 0.04 the pass-through is 1/(1+0.04*0.68) = 0.973, and the same 32% log drop yields ~31% more inelastic — nearly three times the headline — while the "strategic competition offsets two-thirds" claim evaporates entirely (offset ~3%). The entire quantitative content of both halves of the abstract rests on one instrument. And that instrument, eq. (24), is not external: Ê_agg,k is the model's own elasticity equilibrium solved under counterfactual equal-weighted portfolios, and it contains chi and the estimated Ē_jk themselves, recovered as a fixed point. The authors' defense — "This is not an issue for identification as parameters are by definition not endogenous" — is a formal dodge. A model-generated instrument's exclusion restriction is untestable and inherits every functional-form assumption (logit demand, E_ik = Ē_i − chi*E_agg linear in E_agg, E_1i and zeta loading on log book equity only). The authors read rows 15–16 as evidence that endogeneity correction matters; a referee reads the same rows as an OLS-vs-IV gap of a factor of ~75 with no external instrument to arbitrate.

B. "PASSIVE" IS MODEL-DEFINED, AND THE DIRECTION OF THE RESULT IS PARTLY DEFINITIONAL. Appendix IA D.3: an investor is passive iff their fixed KY-style elasticity E_i^fixed < kappa, with kappa = 0.06 chosen "to calibrate the level of passive investing." Passive investors are then assigned elasticity exactly zero, and |Active_k| is the ownership-weighted complement. The outcome variable E_agg,k is a position-weighted aggregation of exactly those individual elasticities. So "more passive => lower aggregate elasticity" is mechanically true by construction; the only non-tautological content in the paper is the size of chi (the offset). The article must not present the sign as an empirical discovery. Worse, kappa = 0.06 is a free tuning parameter with no reported sensitivity analysis — I found no table varying kappa anywhere in the main text or IA. The entire 19%->41% passive series, hence the entire 32% log drop, hence the entire headline magnitude, floats on an unreported-sensitivity threshold.

C. THE MAGNITUDE IS MEASURE-DEPENDENT BY A FACTOR OF 5–7, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO. HHL's own alternative, the fund-based measure (passive mutual funds + ETFs, +15pp of market cap, a 19% drop in active share), yields 6.3%, not 11% — a 43% reduction from the headline, in the same paper, same page. Going the other way, Behmaram (April 2026, UQAM), "Indexing and the Elasticity of Stock Demand," runs the conceptually parallel counterfactual (freeze passive ownership at its 2000 level) inside a Koijen-Yogo system with an Active-Share-adjusted holdings measure (IXI) and finds aggregate elasticity would be 76% higher (range 64%–100%; 45% in the stock-specific variant). The counterfactuals are not identical objects (level ratio vs. log change; partial equilibrium reduced-form gamma-hat vs. structural equilibrium), so the gap is not a clean contradiction — but a ~7x spread on "how much did passive compress elasticity" across two holdings-based measures is dispositive that 11% is a measurement choice, not a fact. Notably, Behmaram's independent reduced-form bridge estimate of the strategic response, chi-tilde = 3.9 (s.e. 1.7, 95% CI [0.6, 7.3], first-stage F = 308), does loosely corroborate HHL's chi and implies a 27% pass-through at |Active| = 0.68 vs HHL's 33%. So the FRACTION (pass-through ~ one-third) is the corroborated part; the TOTAL (11%) is the fragile part, because it is that fraction times a measurement choice.

D. THE ONLY DESIGN-BASED VALIDATION IS NEAR-TAUTOLOGICAL AND WEAKLY INSTRUMENTED. Table 4 regresses annual log changes in E_agg,k on log changes in |Active_k| and recovers 0.35–0.39, "very close to the theoretical pass-through," including a Russell 1000/2000 index-switching IV in column 5 (coefficient 0.346). Two problems. First, the dependent variable is model-generated FROM chi: eq. (26) implies E_agg,k = [position-weighted mean baseline elasticity] x |Active_k| x 1/(1+chi|Active_k|), so d log E_agg/d log |Active| = 1/(1+chi|Active|) holds IDENTICALLY by construction unless the first bracket co-moves with |Active_k|. The regression therefore tests only for composition shifts; it cannot independently confirm the magnitude of the pass-through. HHL footnote 56 concedes half of this ("statistical significance is not completely meaningful ... because the left-hand-side of the regression is model-generated") but the text nonetheless reads the result as confirmation. Second, the IV column has first-stage F = 9.44 — below the conventional weak-instrument threshold of 10 — on N = 10,619, restricted to CRSP market-cap ranks 500–1500 and to 2007–2020 only, with first-stage effect of only ~5% of active ownership. The paper's one quasi-experiment is thus underpowered, narrow, and pointed at an outcome that already embeds the parameter it purports to validate.

E. VERSION DRIFT IS LARGER THAN THE REPORTED PRECISION. March 2022: chi = 2.15, headline 15%. March 2024 / AER 2025: chi = 2.97, headline 11%. The 2022 abstract said "by about 15%"; the AER abstract says "11 percent." The number moved 27% on identical data (2001–2020, 13F) purely from re-estimation of chi. Decisively: 2.15 lies OUTSIDE the 2024 paper's own robustness band of [2.30, 3.27], and the 2022 version also reported a subsample chi = 1.91. So the paper's own earlier published-as-working-paper estimate would be rejected by its later robustness table. The across-version dispersion in chi (1.91 to 3.27) dwarfs the within-version GMM s.e. of 0.47 and implies a headline range of roughly 9.9% to 13.5%. Specification uncertainty, not sampling uncertainty, is the binding constraint — and none of it is reported as an interval.

F. NO CONFIDENCE INTERVAL IS EVER REPORTED FOR THE 11%. I grepped the full main text and IA: standard errors appear for chi, zeta, and the Table 4/asset-price regressions, never for the counterfactual. The 11% is the product of an estimated parameter (chi, s.e. 0.47), a model-classified data moment (the 81.4%->59.5% active-share path, itself the output of the kappa = 0.06 classification applied to estimated elasticities, with zero propagated error), and a linearization evaluated at the time-average |Active| = 0.68. No uncertainty is propagated through any of it. A single decimal-free point estimate is being asked to carry the article.

G. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY: THIS IS A LONG-RUN, LONG-ONLY, QUARTERLY-SNAPSHOT ELASTICITY, NOT "HOW PRICES RESPOND TO TRADING." Three distinct gaps between the estimand and the article's framing.
  (i) Horizon. van der Beck (HBS WP 26-070, July 2025; JFE 2026), "Short versus Long-run Demand Elasticities in Asset Pricing," shows that elasticities estimated from portfolio LEVELS (exactly HHL's cross-sectional KY-style estimator) sit between short- and long-run elasticities from trades, that long-run elasticities are ~4x short-run (AUM-weighted 1.45 vs 0.37), and that price impacts are ~3x larger at quarterly horizons than in long-run equilibrium. van der Beck explicitly says levels-based elasticities are appropriate for LONG-RUN TREND counterfactuals — which is a partial defense of HHL's 20-year exercise — but it invalidates HHL's own translation of the result into "the price impact of buying $1 of a stock roughly from $2.5 to $2.8." Those are long-run multipliers; the same trade's quarterly price impact is roughly triple in level. The article must not quote $2.5->$2.8 as the price impact of a trade.
  (ii) 13F is long-only US equity, quarter-end. No short positions, no options, no swaps, no intra-quarter trading, no high-frequency/ETF-arbitrage liquidity provision. Precisely the elastic, price-sensitive activity that grew fastest over 2001–2020 is invisible to the estimator. Aggregate demand elasticity as measured is a lower bound on market-wide price sensitivity, and the omitted margin is one that plausibly moved the other way.
  (iii) The cross-sectional holdings estimator recovers the true relative elasticity only under Homogeneous Substitution Conditional on Observables (HCO) — an assumption HHL themselves formalize in companion work and that van der Beck adopts. HHL's conditioning set for elasticity heterogeneity is thin by their own admission: "for the sake of tractability, our baseline analysis only includes book equity in the determination of the individual elasticity and the reference price" (E_1i and zeta restricted to zero on all dimensions but book equity). One characteristic is a slender basis for "stocks are equally good substitutes conditional on observables."

H. SAMPLE COVERAGE AND THE ONE-INVESTOR HOUSEHOLD RESIDUAL. 13F covers 80% of market cap; the remaining ~20% is a "residual household sector" that mixes direct household holdings, sub-$100m managers, some foreign investors, and any manager holding fewer than 100 stocks, and is modeled as A SINGLE INVESTOR purely to force shares to add up (App. IA D.4, following Koijen-Yogo). Whatever elasticity the system assigns that composite entity mechanically enters E_agg,k and enters the |Active_k| denominator. A fifth of the market is a modeling convenience, and the paper reports no sensitivity to how it is handled. Additional filters compound this: stocks with fewer than 20 managers are pushed into the outside asset, as are share codes 12/18 and any stock with missing characteristics.

I. THE COUNTERFACTUAL EXPLICITLY HOLDS EVERYTHING ELSE FIXED, AND THE PAPER SHOWS THAT "EVERYTHING ELSE" MOVED A LOT. HHL concede "the rise of passive investing is not a purely exogenous phenomenon" and justify exogeneity by appeal to plausibility (cheaper index technology, ETFs, investors "listening to finance professors"). More damaging for the article's framing, Section 6.2 finds a SECOND, comparably large driver: the investor-specific component of active investors' elasticity rose to 2007 then trended down and "dropped overall," and average aggregate elasticity fell 0.41 -> 0.27 (a ~34% decline) over the sample — roughly three times the 11% attributed to passive. Passive is, on the paper's own decomposition, a minority contributor to the observed decline in elasticity. Any article sentence implying passive explains the inelasticity of modern markets misreads the paper. Finally the "32% decrease in active investing" is a LOG change (ln(0.595/0.814) = -31.6%); the simple percentage drop is 27.2%. A reader taking 32% as a level change is wrong.

WHY NOT VETO. Peer-reviewed at AER, public replication package, 16-specification robustness table that the authors did not hide (including the two rows that most damage them), correctly-signed and externally loosely-corroborated pass-through (Behmaram's chi-tilde = 3.9 CI includes 2.97), and a magnitude that is stable at 10–12% across every specification in the paper's preferred identified family. The direction is not in doubt and the paper is honest about its own limits. VETO would be a misuse of the power.

WHY NOT SINGLE_SOURCE_OK EITHER. Because the article, per the task description, wants to use this as "its best-identified causal magnitude." It is not a causal magnitude in the design-based sense at all: it is an in-model comparative static whose two inputs are (a) a parameter identified solely by a model-generated instrument that, when removed, drives the parameter to zero, and (b) a passive share defined by an untested threshold that moves the answer from 6.3% to 11% to (under an alternative holdings measure) something several times larger. The phrase "best-identified causal magnitude" is the specific claim I am rejecting; the number itself can survive under the conditions below.

It is an in-model comparative static from a structurally estimated demand system, not a design-based causal estimate. Correct framing: 'the most careful structural estimate available' or 'the best-identified estimate of the OFFSET (how much competing investors absorb), which is roughly one-third pass-through.'

Lead with the fraction, not the total. The pass-through of ~1/3 (competition offsets ~2/3) is the paper's real, externally corroborated contribution — Behmaram's independent reduced-form bridge gives chi-tilde = 3.9 (95% CI [0.6, 7.3]) implying a 27% pass-through at the same active share vs HHL's 33%. The 11% total is that fraction multiplied by a contested measurement of how much passive grew, and is the fragile half.

Always attach the range, never the bare point estimate. Minimum acceptable form: '11% under HHL's broad, model-based measure of passive; 6.3% under their narrower fund-based measure (passive mutual funds + ETFs).' Both numbers are in the same paper on the same page. Quoting only 11% is cherry-picking the larger one.

State explicitly that 'passive' here is model-defined, not observed: an institution is classified passive if its estimated Koijen-Yogo fixed elasticity falls below a threshold kappa = 0.06 that the authors chose 'to calibrate the level of passive investing.' No sensitivity analysis to kappa appears anywhere in the paper or its appendix. This threshold generates the entire 19%->41% passive series and therefore the entire magnitude.

Do not present the SIGN as an empirical finding. Passive investors are assigned elasticity exactly zero and the outcome (aggregate elasticity) is a position-weighted average of individual elasticities, so 'more passive => less elastic' is true by construction. reasoning:
SUMMARY OF THE HUNT

The claim has two halves and they do not survive equally. (A) The DESCRIPTIVE half — "the amount of earnings information impounded before the announcement fell over 1990–2019" — has genuine independent multi-source support. (B) The CAUSAL/ATTRIBUTIONAL half — "and passive ownership did it, at a magnitude of ~1/4 of the whole-sample mean" — is contested by independent measurements, including one that uses Sammon's OWN headline measure and gets the opposite sign, and one that uses Sammon's OWN identification setting and gets a null. On (B) I found roughly as many independent same-data-different-team results pointing away as pointing toward. Hence DIRECTION_CONTESTED rather than UPGRADE_MULTISOURCE.

=== I. INDEPENDENT SAME-DIRECTION MEASUREMENTS (different team AND different data) ===

1. Israeli, Lee & Sridharan, "Is there a dark side to exchange traded funds? An information perspective," Review of Accounting Studies 22(3), 2017, 1048–1083. Different team (Technion/Stanford/Emory), different data (ETF ownership panel, ~2000–2014), different construct: FUTURE earnings response coefficient (FERC) — literally how much of next period's earnings news is already in today's return. They find ETF ownership → FERC DECLINES, analyst coverage declines, return synchronicity rises, spreads widen. This is the closest independent construct match to "prices anticipate earnings less" and it is same-direction. Strongest genuine corroboration I found.

2. Bennett, Stulz & Wang, "Does joining the S&P 500 index hurt firms?" NBER WP 27593 (2020), published JFE. Different team (Tulane/Ohio State/Lancaster), different data/design (S&P 500 additions 1997–2017), different measure (GPIN, Duarte-Hu-Young; plus R²). Text of the paper (§6.1, local copy) states GPIN decreases with index addition, and that regressing informativeness directly on passive mutual-fund holdings shows "strong evidence" that passive holdings reduce GPIN. Same direction.

3. Höfler, Schlag & Schmeling, "Passive Investing and Market Quality," working paper March 2025 (Goethe Frankfurt / SAFE / CEPR; AFA 2025, SFS Cavalcade 2024). Different team, different data (US ETF ownership + index reconstitutions), different measures (reversal persistence, spreads, idiosyncratic vol, tail risk, variance decomposition). Finding: higher passive ETF ownership "reduces the importance of firm-specific information for returns but increases the importance of transitory noise." Same direction, adjacent construct.

4. Qin & Singal, "Indexing and Stock Price Efficiency," Financial Management 44(4), 2015, 875–904. Independent team/data; indexing → lower price efficiency. Same direction (Sammon cites it himself as such).

5. Martineau, "Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift," Critical Finance Review, 2022 (local full text). Independent team (Toronto), independent data (Compustat 1973–2019 + I/B/E/S 1984–2019, 593,654 announcements). Explicitly documents that "pre-announcement drifts have also significantly weakened over time" and that announcement-date prices are now effectively martingale. This is an independent confirmation of the DESCRIPTIVE fact Sammon's |Ret| / pre-earnings-drift results rest on — but Martineau's own candidate explanation is Reg FD (2000), not passive.

6. Weller, "Does Algorithmic Trading Reduce Information Acquisition?" Review of Financial Studies 31(6), 2018, 2184–2226. Same PJ measure, but genuinely different team and different data (SEC MIDAS market data, 54,879 stock-quarters, ~2012–2014). Finds information in prices falls 9–13% per SD of AT activity, "up to a month before scheduled disclosures." This validates that PJ moves with real information-acquisition frictions — but it assigns the pre-announcement erosion to ALGORITHMIC TRADING. It is a rival attribution, not corroboration of the passive channel. (Sammon controls for Weller's four AT measures in Appendix C.2.2 and reports OLS unchanged — that mitigates but does not settle it, since Weller's AT proxies are 2012–2014-era and Sammon's window is 1990–2019.)

=== II. INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENTS POINTING THE OTHER WAY ===

1. Kacperczyk, Nosal & Sundaresan — SAME PRICE-JUMP MEASURE, OPPOSITE SIGN. Sammon's own footnote 8 (published version) reports that Kacperczyk et al. (2018b) use Weller's PJ and find the MSCI-inclusion shock predicts PJ FALLING by 0.041 and the JGTRRA dividend-tax-cut shock predicts PJ FALLING by 0.225, against a PJ mean of 0.39 and SD of 0.55 — i.e., ownership shocks make prices anticipate earnings MORE. The JGTRRA magnitude (0.225 ≈ 0.4 SD) dwarfs Sammon's effect. Sammon's rebuttal is that these shocks bundle active and passive ownership increases and the active increase is larger — a fair but unresolved point.
   CAVEAT / VERSION DRIFT I VERIFIED: I grepped the Feb-2022 draft, the July-2024 ReStud manuscript, and the current published version of Kacperczyk, Nosal & Sundaresan, "Market Power and Price Informativeness," Review of Economic Studies 92(3), 2025, 1955–1986. "price jump," "Weller," "MSCI," and "JGTRRA" all return ZERO hits in every retrievable version. The PJ counter-result survives only in the superseded 2018 SSRN draft, which I could not retrieve directly; my evidence for it is Sammon's own second-hand report. So this counter-measurement is real but no longer published anywhere citable.
   What the PUBLISHED KNS does say, calibrated to the actual joint growth of institutional size and passive share: "the combination of size and passive share changes gives a relatively stable price informativeness asset by asset," which they call consistent with Bai et al. (2016). A structural model from the team Sammon leans on concludes the observed passive growth is NOT delivering an aggregate informativeness decline.

2. Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg, "On index investing," Journal of Financial Economics 145(3), 2022, 665–683. This is the most damaging item because it is the SAME IDENTIFICATION SETTING. Sammon's primary IV is Russell 1000/2000 rebalancing, and he explicitly adopts CHR's May market-cap proxy, CHR's ±100-rank treated/control cohort construction, and CHR's firm-by-cohort fixed effects (Sammon §4, footnote 10 and eq. 6). CHR, over a 23-year Russell RD sample (1993–2016), find index investing lowers information PRODUCTION (Google searches, EDGAR views, analyst reports) but leaves price informativeness UNCHANGED — and their working-paper abstract is explicit that treated stocks show "no difference in turnover, trading volume, or earnings response coefficients," plus a null on the Hou-Moskowitz semi-strong-form delay measure. Sammon concedes this: in the March-2023 draft he calls CHR "the most closely related paper," and in the published version he lists them under "papers which document no relationship between passive ownership and price informativeness." So: same instrument, same universe, different informativeness constructs, opposite conclusion. Whether Sammon's result is a real finding or a measure-selection artifact within the Russell design is genuinely open.

3. Hu & Liang, "Passive Institutional Ownership and the Informational Efficiency of Stock Prices," Journal of Accounting, Auditing & Finance, March 2026. Independent team (Syracuse), S&P 500 addition shock — one of Sammon's own two IVs. Finding: passive ownership → more firm disclosure → HIGHER earnings response coefficients and WEAKER PEAD, interpreted as FASTER incorporation of earnings information. Note the interpretive collision: a bigger announcement-day price move per unit surprise is Sammon's evidence of DEGRADED anticipation and Hu-Liang's evidence of IMPROVED efficiency. The same sign, two opposite readings, with a disclosure mechanism Sammon never tests.

4. Glosten, Nallareddy & Zou, "ETF Activity and Informational Efficiency of Underlying Securities," Management Science 67(1), 2021, 22–47. Independent team (Columbia/Duke/HBS), different data. ETF activity → increased informational efficiency, specifically improved incorporation of ACCOUNTING information (i.e., earnings) into prices, concentrated in systematic information. Opposite direction on the earnings-information channel.

5. Kacperczyk, Sundaresan & Wang, "Do Foreign Investors Improve Market Efficiency?" NBER WP 24765 (2018), RFS 2021. usageConditions: The MECHANISM may be stated as multi-sourced. Acceptable framing: 'Several independent research teams, using different data, find that demand which arrives in proportion to index weight pushes up the relative prices of the biggest index members — the largest stocks face the most inelastic residual demand (Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche, AER 2025), and the Bank of Japan's ETF program produced exactly this distortion in Japan, visibly enough that the BoJ abandoned the price-weighted Nikkei 225 for the cap-weighted TOPIX.'

The 29% figure must NOT be load-bearing. It is a linear cumulation, by the authors themselves, of a single contemporaneous quarterly coefficient that the same authors write 'can partly mean-revert,' and it is roughly 7x their own structural calibration's 0-4% range. If it appears at all, it must appear WITH the 0-4% calibration figure in the same sentence and with the mean-reversion caveat attributed to the authors. Never write '29%' or '30%' as a standalone finding.

If the gradient's numbers are quoted, quote the whole gradient including its collapse: top-10 +0.687%/qtr (t=2.46) down through top-50 +0.528%, top-100 +0.303%, top-150 +0.208%, to top-200 +0.145% which is NOT statistically significant (t=1.64). The article must not stop at the top-10 and top-50 numbers.

Any sentence attributing the Magnificent Seven's rise, or current US market concentration, to passive flows must carry the countervailing evidence in the same passage — specifically Bye, Kvaerner & Werker (2026) that today's top-7 share is within norms seen from the 1930s to the 1960s and that the US is not more concentrated than peer developed markets despite having the world's highest passive share, and GMO's (Inker & Pease, 2Q 2024) finding that the mega-cap performance gap unexplained by fundamentals is 'quite small.'

Do not cite Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche (2025) as unqualified support. Their Figure 3 supports the size gradient, but their headline estimate is that twenty years of rising passive made individual-stock demand only 11% more inelastic, with strategic reaction offsetting two-thirds of the mechanical effect. Citing their figure while omitting their headline reproduces JVZ's selective use.

Do not present Vanguard's mid-cap-ownership finding as a refutation of JVZ. It rebuts a different (strawman) mechanism — 'index funds own outsize megacap stakes' — whereas JVZ require only cap-proportional demand plus inelastic large-cap residual supply. If the article mentions the Vanguard figure, it must say why it does not bite.

The article must acknowledge the strongest opposing measurement somewhere in the same section: Greenwood & Sammon (JF 2025) find the S&P 500 addition effect collapsed from 7.4% in the 1990s to 0.3% in the last decade even as index-linked assets soared — the opposite of the time trend JVZ's mechanism predicts. Omitting this while presenting JVZ as 'the best-credentialed evidence' would be a material one-sidedness.

If the article characterizes JVZ as 'best-credentialed,' that phrase must be scoped to the mechanism, not the magnitude — e.g. 'the best-credentialed evidence for the channel' rather than 'for the size of the distortion.' No independent estimate of the cumulative wedge exists in either direction.

Flag for the METHOD_AUDIT seat and for any hedging language: PassiveFlow is a change in a ratio whose denominator is index market capitalization — a price — measured contemporaneously with the dependent-variable return. Wardlaw (JF 2020) is the published demonstration that this exact class of construction mechanically embeds the realized return and that results in that literature do not survive purging it. I found no indication JVZ address this.
